extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in literary theory, criticism, and creative-writing practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria on memory, association of ideas, national literary character, and stylistic qualities useful for evaluating or producing literary works. Emphasizes cognitive foundations (memory/imagination), associative techniques, tonal consistency, and distinctions between style and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory as a mode of Imagination and modification of Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Memory, then, as commonly understood, is the faculty of preserving and recalling mental representations, together with the consciousness that they have been presented to the mind before: and in this sense it is obviously a mode of the Imagination, which is in general 'the faculty of representing an object without the presence of it in the intuition;' although likewise a 'modification of the Judgment, inasmuch as it judges of present thoughts and images that they are the same as past ones.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat memory not merely as archival recall but as an imaginative faculty that supplies images for composition and as a judging faculty that recognizes identity. When composing, consider how remembered images function imaginatively and how awareness of repetition or sameness affects meaning and reader recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing recalled unless previously deposited (prior impressions required)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nothing can be recalled in the mind unless its elements have already been deposited there in the form of ideas...”—(Locke/Aquinas reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a writer, ensure the necessary sensory or conceptual elements are introduced (deposited) before expecting readers to recall or infer them later. Use early 'impressions' to enable later recollection, echoes, or motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of ideas as the general principle of recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory’s principle for recalling ideas is the same as 'the general principle of the association of ideas'—ideas become associated and recalled through various relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use associative links (semantic, sensory, spatial, temporal, causal) to guide a reader's recollection and build motifs. Deliberate arrangement of impressions will control how associations are formed and how recollection unfolds in the reader's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five occasions/causes of recollection (association): nearness, likeness, contrast, cause/effect, contiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge (and commentators cited) treats several 'occasioning causes of recollections' or 'sorts of connexions of ideas'—noting nearness in time and space, likeness (resemblance), contrariety/contrast, and cause and effect as influential principles of association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing associative chains in a text, exploit these relations deliberately: spatial/temporal proximity, similarity, contrast/opposition, and causation. These are practical levers for mnemonic design, image recurrence, and thematic linkage. Beware reducing all to a single principle; each exerts distinct influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of impressions governs recollection (mnemonic string/propinquity metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recollection 'depends on the order of the motions left in the mind from the first impression'; objects are 'strung together, like beads, upon the string of propinquity or relationship'—we follow the string to arrive at the particular bead (memory) desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange initial impressions in an order that will yield the desired recollection path. For mnemonic or associative effects, think of sequences as a string: the order determines which images or ideas will be reached when a reader follows associative cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial memory depends on association
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial (mnemonic) memory 'depends wholly upon association, and association itself also depends on memory'—the two are intertwined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ learned mnemonic devices (images, loci, ordered sequences) rooted in associative principles to structure narrative memory—use concrete linked images or loci to help readers or characters recall complex information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory works in conjunction with other cognitive powers (phantasy/imagination and judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory 'comes into act only in conjunction with other powers of the mind; its relation to phantasy or imagination is implied... and it is plainly stated by Aristotle'—memory is connected to phantasm/imagery and to intellectual representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with awareness that remembered images interact with imaginative invention and judgment. Use memory both as raw material for imaginative recombinations and as evaluative context that readers use to judge identity and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing grotesque/trivial with serious or sacred subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency 'to bring the grotesque and the trivial into connexion with serious and sacred subjects has been called
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tonal incongruity: when handling sacred or solemn material, do not undermine it by inserting grotesque or trivial elements unless intentionally seeking satirical or destabilizing effect. Coleridge notes this mixture as a cultural 'disease' and a stylistic fault in some periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and character consistency within a work
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Hans Sachs's Cain drama where 'the first and last parts of this piece are not very congruous with each other'—early scenes show a 'naughty good for nothing boy' while the last act presents the 'awful and adult Cain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain congruity of tone and character development across a work. Abrupt, unmotivated shifts between comic/juvenile and tragic/adult registers will disrupt credibility and aesthetic effect unless carefully justified by the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style vs. substance: polished diction does not substitute for strength of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: On Opitz: 'The reputation of Opitz, perhaps, surpassed his merits, as it reposed rather on polish of diction than on strength of thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize conceptual depth and thoughtfulness over mere surface elegance. Diction polish enhances reception but cannot substitute for substantive ideas; evaluate (or write) works by both their verbal craft and the force of their thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirable authorial qualities: distinct purpose, masculine character, chastened style
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism observed that 'the parent vice of German Literature is want of distinct purpose; and, as consequences of this, want of masculine character and chastened style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clarity of purpose and disciplined, restrained expression. A well-defined aim and a controlled, robust stylistic approach are presented as markers of literary excellence; absence of these traits is criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value originality, exploration, and pure intellectual activity over pseudo‑practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge contrasts a 'pseudo-practicality' (English vice: everything must 'issue in something to be done, forthwith and outwardly') with the German tendency to 'care more for pure intellectual activity' and 'go exploring in all directions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage exploratory, speculative writing that enlarges intellectual territory rather than always aiming for immediate practical effect or didactic utility. Original discovery and intellectual ambition are positively appraised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coleridge’s national typology of intellectual and stylistic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge's comparative table: e.g., GERMANY — 'Genius, Talent, Fancy' ; ENGLAND — 'Genius, Sense, Humor' ; FRANCE — 'Cleverness, Talent, Wit'. Forms/effects: GERMANY 'Idea or Law Anticipated', ENGLAND 'Law Discovered', FRANCE 'Theory invented'. Also contrasts 'Totality, Selection, Particularity' and 'Distinctness, Clearness, Palpability', and temporal orientations: GERMANY 'Past and Future', ENGLAND 'Past and Present', FRANCE 'The Present.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these typological distinctions as heuristics for evaluating national tendencies in literature (style, aim, intellectual orientation). They suggest which qualities are prized or dominant in different literary traditions and help in assessing a work's character in a comparative context; treat as general tendencies, not absolute rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, argumentative power, and erudition as virtues (Lessing example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing is praised as 'far greater as a critic and polemic than as a poet, and wrote in an admirably clear style, and with considerable power of thought and erudition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value clear expression, rigorous argument, and learned grounding in critical writing. For prose and critical genres especially, lucidity and intellectual force are central evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter, simplicity, and popular effect (Hans Sachs example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hans Sachs's style: 'simple in thought and expression, but easy and flowing; the metre, short and ballad-like, generally the eight or nine syllable iambic with rhyme.' His poems were 'received with noisy approbation' for their popular turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for popular appeal, employ straightforward diction, flowing phrasing, and accessible metrical patterns (ballad-like iambics). Match formal choices (meter, rhyme, diction) to intended audience and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of classical and foreign models to ennoble material
rubrics_metrics.description: Opitz and others 'sought to ennoble and dignify the romantic material, by models selected from the ancients and the Italians... From the last he borrowed the sonnet and melo-drama; the ancients he imitated in didactic and lyric poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate borrowing/adaptation of classical or foreign forms (sonnet, melodrama, epic devices) can elevate material, but must suit the writer's powers and the subject. Use models as resources, not as mere imitation; beware being 'without imitators' or lacking original force when over-dependent on models.
